article_title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
citation: Bond, M., Khosravi, H., De Laat, M., Bergdahl, N., Negrea, V., Oxley, E., Pham, P., Chong, S. W. & Siemens, G. (2024). A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00436-z
title: Zawacki-Richter et al.'s (2019) four-area AIEd typology used as the review's organising classification
description: This typology classifies AI-in-education research into four broad areas: Profiling and prediction, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, Assessment and Evaluation, and Adaptive Systems and Personalisation. The tertiary review adopted it as the starting coding frame, stating it coded the corpus "using Zawacki-Richter et al. 's (2019) typology ... as a starting point", with reviews not specifying a focus coded as General AIEd. Each area is substantively described in the article, e.g. Profiling and Prediction covers dropout prediction and student models, while Adaptive Systems and Personalisation covers tailored content delivery and personalised learning pathways.
requirements: Reviews must be classifiable by their purported focus within title, abstract, keywords or search terms; reviews without a specified focus are coded General AIEd
constraints: The typology was developed for AIEd research generally and applied here to higher-education evidence syntheses; some reviews spanned multiple areas and were coded under both focus and key-findings categories
target_learning_goals: mapping applications of AI in formal higher education teaching, learning, and administration
examples: The review coded all 66 corpus reviews by primary focus under this typology, producing Table 5 counts (General AIEd 31, Profiling and Prediction 19, Adaptive Systems and Personalisation 18, Assessment and Evaluation 3, Intelligent Tutoring Systems 1)
key_sources: Bond, M., Khosravi, H., De Laat, M., Bergdahl, N., Negrea, V., Oxley, E., Pham, P., Chong, S. W. & Siemens, G. (2024). A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00436-z

article_title: Effects of group experience and information distribution on collaborative learning
citation: Jimmy Zambrano, Femke Kirschner, John Sweller, Paul A. Kirschner. (2019). Effects of group experience and information distribution on collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09495-0
title: Task-based collective schema account: prior collaborative experience builds a domain group schema that regulates transactional activities and optimizes collaborative cognitive load
description: The article explains its findings through cognitive load theory extended to groups. It proposes that when group members solve domain-specific tasks together they build shared schemas of joint work, and that "this group experience may be a domain group schema (i.e., a generalized domain skill at group level) that is stored in long-term memory to solve similar learning problems". Once acquired, such schemas serve as internalized guidance that regulates transactional activities — the communication and coordination specific to collaboration — and thereby optimize the collaborative cognitive load, so that working memory resources can be invested in constructing high-order schemas of the learning task rather than in unproductive inter-individual activity.
requirements: Prior collaborative experience with tasks similar to the learning tasks, so that task- or domain-based collaborative schemas can be formed and activated
constraints: The article states collaborative learning is not general knowledge applicable to any domain indiscriminately: it is better to prepare learners to collaborate according to particular characteristics of a task or domain
target_learners: Novice secondary school students learning high-complexity tasks in 3-person groups
target_learning_goals: Complex problem solving (break-even point problems) tested by individual short-term and delayed retention
examples: Experience groups trained over four sessions on quadratic equations with distributed equation values (e.g., for −15x2, each member received −5x2) before collaborating on break-even problems
key_sources: Jimmy Zambrano, Femke Kirschner, John Sweller, Paul A. Kirschner. (2019). Effects of group experience and information distribution on collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09495-0

article_title: Reflections on the Ecolab and the Zone of Proximal Development
citation: Rosemary Luckin & Benedict du Boulay. (2016). Reflections on the Ecolab and the Zone of Proximal Development. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0072-x
title: Zone of Available Assistance (ZAA) and Zone of Proximal Adjustment (ZPA) as an operationalization of Vygotsky's ZPD
description: The article introduces the ZAA and ZPA as two additional concepts introduced to clarify the ZPD for software implementation. The ZAA describes the variety of resources available within a learner's world, while the ZPA is created from a sub-set of the resources from the ZAA and should represent the resources that most accurately match a learner's needs. A More-Able Partner works with the learner to select optimal resources from the ZAA to create the learner's ZPA. Assistance must be flexible, quantifiable, and capable of being increased and decreased.
requirements: Assistance offered to a learner must be flexible and capable of being increased and decreased, and must therefore be quantifiable.
constraints: The ZPD concept as originally introduced lacked specificity about the type of assistance that should be offered to learners, how it should be quantified and how it should be provided and withdrawn.
target_learning_goals: Food webs and food chains (science curriculum)
key_sources: Rosemary Luckin & Benedict du Boulay. (2016). Reflections on the Ecolab and the Zone of Proximal Development. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0072-x

article_title: Brazilian dentists' knowledge, skills, and attitudes towards minimal intervention dentistry: development and psychometric analysis.
citation: de Moura Regina Cardoso, Perazzo Matheus França, Leal Soraya Coelho, Maia Lucianne Cople, Massignan Carla. (2026). Brazilian dentists’ knowledge, skills, and attitudes towards minimal intervention dentistry: development and psychometric analysis. Brazilian Oral Research. https://doi.org/10.1590/1807-3107bor-2026.vol40.039
title: Competencies conceptualized as knowledge, skills, and attitudes based on Zarifian's framework
description: The article conceptualizes competencies as the integration of knowledge, skills, and attitudes, based on Zarifian's framework, which defines competencies across three dimensions: knowledge (knowing), skills (know-how), and attitudes (willingness to act). Competency-related items were organized into thematic areas aligned with the four core concepts of MID proposed by Walsh: recognition, reduction, regeneration, and repair. This framework underpinned the theoretical division of the scale into a knowledge factor and a skills-and-attitudes factor.
requirements: Competency items must be organized into thematic areas aligned with the four core concepts of MID
constraints: The framework was applied within the domain of Minimal Intervention Dentistry for dental caries management
target_learning_goals: understanding competency as integration of knowledge, skills, and attitudes
key_sources: de Moura Regina Cardoso, Perazzo Matheus França, Leal Soraya Coelho, Maia Lucianne Cople, Massignan Carla. (2026). Brazilian dentists’ knowledge, skills, and attitudes towards minimal intervention dentistry: development and psychometric analysis.
